newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria votes for new president amid deep crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria votes for new president amid deep crisis.

text.p: Bulgarians vote in a presidential election on Sunday with their country in the grip of a deep economic crisis and a crime wave marked by the killing of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.
President Zhelyu Zhelev, 61, Bulgaria's first non-communist head of state, is not standing for re-election for the largely ceremonial post.
The two front-runners are lawyer Petar Stoyanov, candidate of the united opposition who beat Zhelev in a U.S.-style primary in June, and socialist Culture Minister Ivan Marazov.

But the outcome of the election may be crucial for Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, whose position as Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) leader has been shaken by his government's inability to handle the crisis, analysts say.

"The main battle will begin after the presidential elections. For me the greatest challenge will be to get the BSP out of parliament," Ivan Kostov, leader of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces, told the daily Standard in an interview published on Thursday.

The former Warsaw Pact country of nine million is in the grip of a severe economic crisis and a poverty spiral which has robbed many Bulgarians of their faith in the political system. Many say they will simply not vote.
It has the lowest level of foreign investment of any country in the region and a quarter of its numerous and insolvent banks are in receivership.

The central bank is rapidly running out of money to prop up the lev and buy fuel and also wheat -- to replace Bulgarian production which was exported because the world price is higher than the local price.
Inflation is forecast to exceed 200 percent this year.
High interest rates introduced to stabilise the banking system have doubled internal debt. Foreign exchange reserves have plunged to about $505 million from about $1.5 billion over one year .

An International Monetary Fund mission is due in Sofia next week to discuss a policy framework that would allow the fund to release a twice-delayed $115 million second tranche of funding under Bulgaria's standby accord.
Though polls show Stoyanov ahead of nearest rival Marazov, he is short of an absolute majority in the first round.
He says he would cooperate with any government trying to end the crisis but has raised the possibility of early parliamentary elections.
"If I win this election, there will be a new political situation in the country because this will be a vote against the BSP," he told a television debate on Tuesday.

Violent crime is rising with poverty though the killing of ex-premier Lukanov had strong political overtones. Lukanov was shot dead in front of his home on October 2 in an apparent contract killing so far unsolved.
A Socialist colleague of Lukanov, Andrei Raichev, said the former premier had been about to expose high-level corruption within the Socialist government when he was murdered.

"This was an act of political confrontation. I believe that whatever the motives were we should call it an act of political terrorism, and I hope it will be the last act of political violence," Socialist presidential candidate Marazov said.

A total of 13 pairs of presidential and vice-presidential candidates are contesting the election. If no candidate wins more than 50 percent of votes in the first round, a second round will be held a week later.
